lower-0862-s7-explain-with-models.description: Use a number line, a bar and pairs of counters to explain a short calculation.

sections.title: Where did you finish?
sections.label: Trace a move
sections.intro: Mark the starting level first. For each lift move, find a new level on the line. Then compare the route with the distance between its ends.

blocks.html: Going up adds to the current level. Going down subtracts. To count the total distance, add the lengths of all moves.

figure.alt: A number line showing a move from −3 to 2 and then to −1.
figure.caption: The route has length 8. It finishes 2 levels above the start.

blocks.prompt:
A lift starts on level -9. It goes up 9 levels and then down 4 levels. Level 0 is the entrance.

Which level does the lift reach?
blocks.hint: Use the sign of each move and add it to the current level.
blocks.solution:
A move up adds 9. After that move the lift is on level 0.

A move down subtracts 4. \(0-4=-4\)

\(-4\)

retry.feedback: The last move is down. Subtract its distance from the level reached after the first move.

blocks.html: The last level can be negative even when the distance travelled is positive. These numbers answer different questions.

blocks.prompt:
A lift starts on level -2. It goes up 10 levels and then down 4 levels. Level 0 is the entrance.

Which level does the lift reach?
blocks.hint: Use the sign of each move and add it to the current level.
blocks.solution:
A move up adds 10. After that move the lift is on level 8.

A move down subtracts 4. \(8-4=4\)

\(4\)

retry.feedback: The last move is down. Subtract its distance from the level reached after the first move.

blocks.html: Show one calculation for the finishing level and another for the distance travelled.

sections.title: Which parts make the whole?
sections.label: Count the whole
sections.intro: Draw one block for each part and make all blocks the same size. Label colours before counting.

blocks.html: A fraction compares some equal parts with all the equal parts. Another complete batch keeps that fraction the same.

figure.alt: A strip with two blue and three yellow blocks of equal size.
figure.caption: Count all five equal parts before finding the fraction that is blue.

blocks.prompt:
Each batch for a school event has 2 blue bands and 4 yellow bands. The organisers pack 36 bands using whole batches.

How many bands are blue?
blocks.hint: Divide by the total in one batch. Then count the blue bands.
blocks.solution:
Each batch has 6 bands. There are \(36\div 6=6\) batches.

There are 2 blue bands in each batch. Multiply by 6.

\(12\)

retry.feedback: You counted the yellow bands. Use the blue part of each batch.

blocks.html: Using the number of yellow parts as the denominator would compare blue to yellow, rather than blue to the whole.

blocks.prompt:
Each batch for a school event has 3 blue bands and 5 yellow bands. The organisers pack 48 bands using whole batches.

How many bands are blue?
blocks.hint: Divide by the total in one batch. Then count the blue bands.
blocks.solution:
Each batch has 8 bands. There are \(48\div 8=6\) batches.

There are 3 blue bands in each batch. Multiply by 6.

\(18\)

retry.feedback: You counted the yellow bands. Use the blue part of each batch.

blocks.html: Draw the whole bar and count the parts before calculating.

sections.title: Will there always be a spare?
sections.label: Look for a spare
sections.intro: Try one small case with counters first. Then ask what happens when a complete pair is added.

blocks.html: A pair adds two. When an odd number of singles is added, the complete display still has one item left after pairing.

figure.alt: Three pairs of blue counters and one unpaired amber counter.
figure.caption: Making another pair leaves the single counter unpaired.

blocks.prompt:
A display has 8 pairs of books and 5 single books on a shelf.

How many books are in the display?
blocks.hint: Count two objects per pair before adding the singles.
blocks.solution:
There are two in each pair. Multiply 8 by 2, then add the 5 singles.

\(21\)

retry.feedback: A pair has two objects. Double the number of pairs first.

blocks.html: Several examples can suggest a rule. Explain what changing the number of pairs does to the spare item.

blocks.prompt:
A display has 9 pairs of books and 5 single books on a shelf.

How many books are in the display?
blocks.hint: Count two objects per pair before adding the singles.
blocks.solution:
There are two in each pair. Multiply 9 by 2, then add the 5 singles.

\(23\)

retry.feedback: A pair has two objects. Double the number of pairs first.

blocks.html: A reason about any number of pairs earns more than a list of separate examples.

examples.title: A route between floors
examples.question:
A lift starts on level -5. It goes up 7 levels and then down 3 levels. Level 0 is the entrance.

  1. Which level does the lift reach?

    [2]

  2. How many levels does the lift travel in total?

    [2]

  3. Describe one move that returns the lift to its starting level.

    [2]
solution: (a) A move up adds 7. After that move the lift is on level 2.
A move down subtracts 3. \(2-3=-1\)
(b) Both moves add to the distance travelled. Add the lengths 7 and 3.
(c) Compare the finishing level -1 with the starting level -5.
Go down 4 levels.

examples.title: A route between floors
examples.question:
A lift starts on level -6. It goes up 7 levels and then down 3 levels. Level 0 is the entrance.

  1. Which level does the lift reach?

    [2]

  2. How many levels does the lift travel in total?

    [2]

  3. Describe one move that returns the lift to its starting level.

    [2]
solution: (a) A move up adds 7. After that move the lift is on level 1.
A move down subtracts 3. \(1-3=-2\)
(b) Both moves add to the distance travelled. Add the lengths 7 and 3.
(c) Compare the finishing level -2 with the starting level -6.
Go down 4 levels.

examples.title: Two colours, one batch
examples.question:
Each batch for a school event has 2 blue bands and 3 yellow bands. The organisers pack 20 bands using whole batches.

  1. How many bands are blue?

    [2]

  2. What fraction of the whole batch is blue? Give your answer in simplest form.

    [2]

  3. A volunteer packs 15 yellow bands. How many blue bands should go with them?

    [2]
solution: (a) Each batch has 5 bands. There are \(20\div 5=4\) batches.
There are 2 blue bands in each batch. Multiply by 4.
(b) Use 2 blue bands over 5 bands altogether, then simplify.
(c) Divide the yellow count by 3 to find the new number of batches. Each batch needs 2 blue bands.

examples.title: Two colours, one batch
examples.question:
Each batch for a school event has 3 blue bands and 4 yellow bands. The organisers pack 28 bands using whole batches.

  1. How many bands are blue?

    [2]

  2. What fraction of the whole batch is blue? Give your answer in simplest form.

    [2]

  3. A volunteer packs 20 yellow bands. How many blue bands should go with them?

    [2]
solution: (a) Each batch has 7 bands. There are \(28\div 7=4\) batches.
There are 3 blue bands in each batch. Multiply by 4.
(b) Use 3 blue bands over 7 bands altogether, then simplify.
(c) Divide the yellow count by 4 to find the new number of batches. Each batch needs 3 blue bands.

examples.title: Pairs and spares
examples.question:
A display has 11 pairs of books and 3 single books on a shelf.

  1. How many books are in the display?

    [2]

  2. The number of pairs changes but the number of singles stays the same. Explain why the total is always odd.

    [2]

  3. Another display of this kind has 37 items. How many pairs are there?

    [2]
solution: (a) There are two in each pair. Multiply 11 by 2, then add the 3 singles.
(b) Group all the items into twos. The singles also leave one unmatched object when put into twos.
Pairs make an even total. The fixed number of singles is odd, so the total is odd.
(c) Remove the 3 singles, then divide the rest by 2.

    [2]
solution: (a) There are two in each pair. Multiply 12 by 2, then add the 3 singles.
(b) Group all the items into twos. The singles also leave one unmatched object when put into twos.
Pairs make an even total. The fixed number of singles is odd, so the total is odd.
(c) Remove the 3 singles, then divide the rest by 2.
